DECK: Discipleship Experience (Section 10) Apologetics

Q1. Which pair of questions does the lesson associate with the biographical test?
A. How many authors produced the document, and how many people witnessed the events described in it?
B. How many manuscripts are available and whether their contents are the same or similar, and how long the interval is between the original and earliest available manuscript?
C. Whether archaeology supports the document, and whether later communities accepted the document as authoritative?
D. Whether the document contains prophecy, and whether the prophecy was fulfilled within the period it describes?
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson assesses manuscript evidence by considering the number and similarity of manuscripts and the interval from the original to the earliest available copies.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — approx. 01:37–06:01

Q2. What does the lesson mean by saying, "A dead God cannot give eternal life"?
A. Eternal life depends on Jesus having conquered death rather than remaining under the power of death.
B. Eternal life can only be received by those who physically witness Jesus' resurrection.
C. Eternal life is possible only when believers are able to prove the resurrection through historical documents.
D. Eternal life depends on believers becoming physically immortal before they can receive salvation.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson connects Jesus’ resurrection with believers’ redemption and future resurrection.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 04:03–05:02
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: John 1:29; Acts 17:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:14

Q3. What does the internal evidence test examine?
A. Whether archaeological discoveries confirm the locations and events described within the Bible.
B. Whether writings outside the Bible confirm the people, places and events described within the Bible.
C. Whether the information within the Bible is coherent and free from known contradictions.
D. Whether the Bible contains more surviving manuscripts than other ancient documents from the same period.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson defines the internal evidence test as examining the Bible’s own testimony for coherence and known contradictions.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 06:41–07:44

Q4. Why does the lesson describe the resurrection as more than simply getting the facts of the past right?
A. It establishes a guarantee concerning the future of those who believe in Jesus.
B. It establishes that every historical detail concerning Jesus can now be independently verified.
C. It establishes that believers will never experience suffering or death after becoming Christians.
D. It establishes that every person who hears the gospel will automatically receive eternal life.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents Jesus’ resurrection as assurance that believers will rise as well.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 04:03–05:46
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: John 1:29; Acts 17:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:14; John 11:25

Q5. Why does the lesson refer to Isaiah's writings about Jesus?
A. Isaiah was written during Jesus' lifetime and records eyewitness testimony about His ministry.
B. Isaiah was discovered as part of the earliest complete New Testament manuscript and confirms the Gospel accounts.
C. Isaiah contains predictions about Jesus' life and death that were written over 700 years before Jesus was born and were later fulfilled.
D. Isaiah proves that Matthew, Mark, Luke and John wrote their Gospel accounts together from the same source.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson cites Isaiah’s predictions about Jesus’ life and death as prophecies written centuries before his birth and later fulfilled.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 10:31–11:39
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Isaiah 53

Q6. Why does the lesson regard the fact that women were the first witnesses of the empty tomb as significant evidence?
A. Women were considered the most reliable legal witnesses in the first-century Jewish world.
B. Women were treated as highly respected public authorities whose testimony was preferred over that of men.
C. Women were treated as second-class citizens in that cultural context, making their inclusion as first witnesses an unlikely choice if the story were fabricated to be convincing.
D. Women were the only people permitted to enter tombs and were automatically considered reliable witnesses.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson argues that reporting women as the first witnesses would have been an unlikely choice for a fabricated account.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD IV — approx. 06:51–09:42
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Luke 24:10

Q7. Which statement best captures the idea that what appears evil or chaotic may not be ultimate?
A. If an event eventually produces something good, the original event should no longer be regarded as evil.
B. If God has a purpose, every event must have been directly caused by Him.
C. A painful or chaotic reality can be genuinely difficult while still not representing the final outcome of God's purpose.
D. Human beings should stop judging circumstances because only God can determine whether something is good.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson says present evil or chaos can be real without being the final outcome of God’s purpose.
REF: THEODICY II — 08:26–09:12

Q8. Why does the lesson consider Jesus' teaching about Himself from Scripture significant?
A. Because Jesus' use of Scripture proves that every surviving biblical manuscript has been preserved perfectly.
B. Because Jesus wrote the Old Testament Himself and could therefore explain every part of it from personal authorship.
C. Because Jesus' teaching about Scripture means that external evidence is no longer necessary for examining the Bible.
D. Because Jesus was the person prophesied about and could teach about Himself from the Scriptures that spoke about Him.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The lesson says Jesus could teach about himself from the Scriptures that prophesied about him.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 10:31–11:39
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Isaiah 53

Q9. What distinction does Hebrews 9 make between Christ's sacrifice and the sacrifices offered by the Old Testament high priest?
A. Christ entered the Most Holy Place repeatedly with His own blood, while the Old Testament high priest entered once a year with animal blood.
B. Christ entered the earthly sanctuary once with His own blood, while the Old Testament high priest entered the heavenly sanctuary repeatedly with animal blood.
C. Christ entered heaven once and for all by His own blood, while the Old Testament high priest repeatedly entered the Most Holy Place with the blood of animals.
D. Christ entered the Most Holy Place every year with His own blood, while the Old Testament high priest offered animal blood only once for Israel.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson contrasts the high priest’s repeated entry with animal blood and Christ’s once-for-all entry into heaven with his own blood.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 00:15–02:35
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: Hebrews 9

Q10. A believer is suffering despite trusting God and wonders whether the suffering means Christ has failed to defeat evil. Which response best reflects the framework presented?
A. The suffering proves that Christ's victory applies only after death and has no present relevance.
B. The suffering shows that the believer has not yet exercised enough faith to appropriate Christ's victory.
C. The suffering exists within the present reality of a fallen world, while Christ's victory guarantees that suffering and death will not have the final word.
D. The suffering should be understood as God's direct method of teaching the believer whatever lesson they have not yet learned.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson connects present suffering with creation’s corruption and presents Christ’s victory as assurance that death and suffering will not have the final word.
REF: THEODICY IV — approx. 00:49–02:59; 14:42–18:23
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Romans 8; Romans 5; John 11:25; 2 Timothy 4; 1 John 5; Revelation 21:4

Q11. What does the lesson mean when it says that the different parties in the Day of Atonement represented one person, Jesus?
A. It means that the high priest, the goats and the other elements were separate sacrifices that were eventually replaced by Jesus.
B. It means that the high priest and the goats were historical figures who physically became Jesus during His ministry.
C. It means that the different elements of the ceremony served as a type and shadow of what Jesus Christ would come to accomplish.
D. It means that Jesus performed the Day of Atonement ceremony in the same form before beginning His earthly ministry.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents the Day of Atonement’s elements as a type and shadow of what Jesus would accomplish.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD I — 12:06–13:42
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Hebrews 9; Leviticus 16

Q12. What does the lesson mean when it describes money as a "spiritual stethoscope"?
A. The amount of money a person has reveals the level of spiritual maturity that person has attained.
B. The way a person responds to money and giving can reveal the condition of that person's heart.
C. The level of financial success a person experiences reveals the strength of that person's relationship with God.
D. The amount of money a person gives determines whether God accepts that person's faith and worship.
ANSWER: B
REF: Not found in the provided sources — N/A

Q13. Why has the problem addressed by theodicy continued to generate questions among Christians and non-Christians?
A. Because Scripture gives no examples of people questioning God's justice
B. Because the existence of evil creates questions about how God's goodness, power and justice relate to human experience
C. Because Christians have historically disagreed about whether God possesses absolute sovereignty
D. Because the Bible presents evil as a mystery that human beings are forbidden to investigate
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson connects the problem of evil with questions about God’s goodness, knowledge, power, and justice.
REF: THEODICY I — approx. 01:18–03:28

Q14. Why does the lesson argue that the Islamic substitution theory conflicts with the earliest historical testimony about Jesus?
A. Because the theory appeared several hundred years after the Christian accounts and conflicts with both Christian and non-Christian testimony concerning His crucifixion.
B. Because the theory appeared before the Christian accounts and therefore contradicts the eyewitnesses who recorded Jesus' crucifixion.
C. Because the theory was developed by Roman authorities who were attempting to explain why Jesus' disciples continued preaching after His death.
D. Because the theory depends entirely on the Gospel accounts while rejecting the historical sources outside the Christian tradition.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson argues that the substitution theory came later and conflicts with earlier Christian and non-Christian testimony about Jesus’ crucifixion.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — approx. 08:15–10:59

Q15. Why does the lesson consider the question "Is the Bible true?" important to the Christian?
A. Because the Bible contains more historical information than every other ancient document.
B. Because the Bible is the oldest religious document available to Christians.
C. Because the Bible is the standard for Christian belief, so questioning its origin and validity raises a question about the foundation of the faith.
D. Because the Bible must be confirmed by archaeological discoveries before Christians can accept its teachings.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson says the Bible is the standard for belief, so questions about its origin and validity affect Christian faith.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 00:29–01:14

Q16. What confidence does the resurrection of Jesus give believers about their own future?
A. It gives believers confidence that they will avoid physical death if they maintain their faith until the end.
B. It gives believers confidence that they will rise again because Jesus Himself rose from the dead.
C. It gives believers confidence that they will experience resurrection only if they have never struggled with doubt.
D. It gives believers confidence that physical death has already ceased to exist for everyone who believes in Jesus.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents Jesus’ resurrection as assurance that believers will rise too.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 04:03–05:46

Q17. What does the lesson highlight about the different backgrounds of the Bible's authors?
A. Their different backgrounds show that the books developed from several unrelated salvation stories.
B. Their different backgrounds suggest that the books were written independently without a common theological direction.
C. Their different backgrounds mean that the books reflect different understandings of salvation that cannot be brought together.
D. Their different backgrounds show that, despite their differences in countries, classes and professions, their writings form a unified salvation story.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The lesson highlights that authors from varied backgrounds contributed to a unified salvation story.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 01:14

Q18. Why was the flood understood as an act of preservation as well as judgment?
A. The corruption of humanity had become so extensive that intervention was necessary to preserve the human race
B. Humanity had become incapable of receiving God's forgiveness and therefore needed to be completely destroyed
C. God needed to demonstrate His authority before establishing His covenant with Noah
D. The flood was primarily intended to punish those who had rejected Noah's preaching
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents the flood as an intervention intended to preserve the human race amid extensive evil.
REF: THEODICY III — approx. 01:49–04:16

Q19. What did the scapegoat represent in the Day of Atonement picture presented in the lesson?
A. It represented the animal whose blood was brought behind the veil to make atonement for the high priest.
B. It represented the one upon whom the sins and rebellious acts of the Israelites were placed before being sent into the wilderness.
C. It represented the high priest who entered the Most Holy Place and returned to announce that the sacrifice had been accepted.
D. It represented the people of Israel who remained outside the tabernacle while the high priest offered sacrifices for their sins.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson says the scapegoat carried the Israelites’ sins away into the wilderness.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD I — 11:18–12:55

Q20. Why does the lesson consider the time interval between an original document and the earliest surviving manuscript?
A. Because the age of the surviving manuscript determines whether its original author was inspired by God.
B. Because a longer interval between manuscripts automatically makes the original document historically unreliable.
C. Because the date of the surviving manuscript determines whether the document's message is doctrinally correct.
D. Because the interval helps us consider how close the surviving evidence is to the period in which the original was written.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The lesson uses the interval to assess how close surviving manuscripts are to the original documents.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 01:37–02:26

Q21. What pattern of divine intervention is identified throughout Scripture?
A. God intervenes whenever His people experience suffering for an extended period
B. God intervenes primarily in ways that advance His overarching will and purpose
C. God intervenes only when human beings have exhausted their own ability to solve a problem
D. God intervenes whenever evil becomes visible enough for humanity to recognize it
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson describes God’s interventions as advancing his overarching will and purpose.
REF: THEODICY III — approx. 00:16–01:49

Q22. What were the differences found in the approximately 5% that did not match in the Isaiah comparison?
A. They involved major changes to the story and theology presented throughout the book of Isaiah.
B. They involved spelling differences, omitted letters and misspelled words that did not change the core meaning.
C. They involved entire sections of Isaiah that had been removed from the later manuscript tradition.
D. They involved different accounts of the life, ministry and death of Jesus within the book of Isaiah.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson characterizes the differences as spelling and copying errors that do not change the core meaning.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 04:02–05:04

Q23. What does Christ's resurrection change about the way death is understood?
A. Death remains the final outcome of human existence but is no longer something Christians should fear
B. Death is no longer the final word for those who belong to Christ because resurrection gives hope beyond physical death
C. Death is removed from the experience of every believer who exercises sufficient faith
D. Death becomes spiritually beneficial because every Christian is guaranteed immediate resurrection after physical death
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents resurrection as hope that death is not the end for believers.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 04:03–05:46

Q24. What does the lesson say Christianity would become without the resurrection?
A. Christianity would become a less effective form of Christianity because its moral teachings would remain unchanged.
B. Christianity would become a mere religion because the resurrection is what distinguishes the Christian faith from a system of moral teaching.
C. Christianity would become a historical movement because the teachings of Jesus would still provide a complete path to eternal life.
D. Christianity would become a different form of Judaism because the death of Jesus would still fulfil the purpose of the Christian faith.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson says the risen Savior, rather than moral teaching alone, distinguishes Christianity.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — 06:27–07:18

Q25. What is the main difference between internal and external evidence in the lesson?
A. Internal evidence examines the Bible's own testimony, while external evidence looks to material outside the Bible to see whether it confirms or denies that testimony.
B. Internal evidence examines the Old Testament, while external evidence examines the New Testament and the events surrounding its development.
C. Internal evidence examines archaeological discoveries, while external evidence examines the prophecies contained within the biblical text.
D. Internal evidence examines Christian belief, while external evidence examines whether non-Christians accept the Bible's historical claims.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson distinguishes evidence drawn from within the Bible from evidence outside it that may confirm or deny its testimony.
REF: IS THE BIBLE TRUE I — 06:41; IS THE BIBLE TRUE II — 00:15–01:10

Q26. What is the lesson's main historical objection to the Islamic substitution theory?
A. The theory emerged several hundred years after Christianity and conflicts with earlier Christian and non-Christian testimony concerning Jesus' crucifixion.
B. The theory emerged before the earliest Christian accounts and therefore represents a competing eyewitness tradition concerning Jesus' death.
C. The theory was based primarily on Roman records that the Christian writers deliberately excluded from their accounts of Jesus.
D. The theory agrees with the earliest historical testimony about Jesus but differs from later Christian interpretations of His death.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson argues that the substitution theory came later and conflicts with earlier testimony about Jesus’ crucifixion.
REF: DID JESUS RISE FROM THE DEAD II — approx. 08:15–10:59

Q27. What is the central purpose of the concept of theodicy as presented?
A. To demonstrate that every form of suffering has an immediately identifiable purpose
B. To defend the goodness and justice of God in response to objections arising from evil
C. To establish that evil exists independently of God's sovereignty
D. To explain why human beings are morally responsible for every form of suffering
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents theodicy as addressing objections to God’s goodness and justice in light of evil.
REF: THEODICY I — approx. 02:11–04:19
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Genesis 18; Exodus 33

Q28. What is the basic claim of the ontological argument as explained in the lesson?
A. God is the greatest possible being, and such a being cannot exist only in the imagination but must exist in reality.
B. God is the first cause of the universe, and therefore everything that exists must ultimately depend on Him.
C. God is the intelligent designer of nature, and the complexity of creation demonstrates that He exists.
D. God is the source of objective morality, and therefore universal moral values demonstrate His existence.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents the argument that the greatest possible being cannot exist only in the imagination and must exist in reality.
REF: IS THERE A GOD III — approx. 06:00–09:51

Q29. Why does Christ's incarnation matter to the question of suffering?
A. God entered human experience and personally experienced hunger, temptation, rejection, suffering and death
B. God entered human experience primarily to demonstrate that suffering is necessary for spiritual maturity
C. God entered human experience so that He could understand human beings despite previously being separated from them
D. God entered human experience to demonstrate that divine power could completely eliminate suffering during earthly life
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The lesson says Christ experienced human pain and temptation, so God is not portrayed as detached from human suffering.
REF: THEODICY IV — approx. 11:12–12:28

Q30. What is the broader purpose of studying apologetics according to the conclusion of the lesson?
A. To equip Christians with enough intellectual arguments to win debates and demonstrate the superiority of Christianity over every opposing belief.
B. To help Christians replace simple faith with intellectual certainty so that difficult questions about Christianity no longer need to be asked.
C. To equip Christians to understand why they believe, engage their minds with their faith, defend it reasonably, and help others come to Christ.
D. To prepare Christians to become academic scholars who can provide technical answers to every philosophical objection against Christianity.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson presents apologetics as preparing Christians to reason about and defend their faith and to help others come to Christ.
REF: IS THERE A GOD III — approx. 10:36–15:41
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Exodus 3; John 8:58; John 1

Q31. How does the lesson define "apologetics"?
A. Apologetics is the religious discipline of defending religious doctrines through systematic argumentation and discourse, derived from the Greek word *apologia* meaning "defense."
B. Apologetics is the practice of repeatedly asking for God's forgiveness for one's doubts.
C. Apologetics is the study of different religions to prove they all worship the same God.
D. Apologetics is the process of apologizing to people of other faiths for historical Christian mistakes.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The speaker defines apologetics, noting it comes from the Greek word "apologia" meaning "defense," and formally defines it as "the religious discipline of defending religious doctrines through systematic argumentation and discourse".
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-c834ed76-9fb4.md (01:56-03:21)

Q32. According to 1 Peter 3:15, as cited in the lesson, who is commanded to give a defense of the faith?
A. Only ordained pastors and church leaders.
B. Only academics and Bible scholars who debate constantly.
C. Only those who are falsely accused in a court of law.
D. Every believer should be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks a reason for their hope.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The speaker quotes 1 Peter 3:15, stating it instructs believers to be ready to give a defense "to everyone who asks you," emphasizing that this applies to everyone "on the streets, in your office, at home," not just academics or scholars.
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-c834ed76-9fb4.md (03:21-04:11)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: 1 Peter 3:15

Q33. What is the core premise of the cosmological argument?
A. The universe is eternal and has always existed in its current form.
B. Whatever begins to exist has a cause, meaning the universe must have a first, uncaused cause that is timeless, changeless, and immaterial.
C. The universe was created by a random combination of gases and matter out of absolute nothingness.
D. The complexity of human DNA proves that the universe was designed by an intelligent being.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The cosmological argument states "whatever begins to exist... has a cause." To avoid an infinite regression, there must be a "first uncaused cause" that is "timeless," "changeless," and "immaterial," which points to God.
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-a563e42b-2b42.md (01:14-03:29)
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Colossians 1:16

Q34. How does the teleological argument use the concept of the "Goldilocks zone" to argue for the existence of God?
A. It shows that Earth's perfect distance from the sun and specific atmospheric gases to sustain life demonstrate precise, intelligent design rather than random chance.
B. It argues that the universe was created from nothing, like a fairy tale.
C. It proves that human fingerprints and DNA evolved naturally over billions of years.
D. It suggests that there are many other habitable planets just like Earth waiting to be discovered.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The teleological argument (intelligent design) uses the "Goldilocks zone" to show that Earth is perfectly positioned—not too hot, not too cold—with a specific combination of gases to support life, arguing that this order cannot result from a random "big bang".
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-a563e42b-2b42.md (10:36-11:42)

Q35. According to the lesson, how does the moral argument demonstrate the existence of God?
A. It proves that morality is entirely subjective and depends solely on an individual's culture.
B. It suggests that humans only behave morally because they fear punishment from human laws.
C. It argues that the existence of objective, universal moral values (like knowing murder is wrong) requires a transcendent moral lawgiver.
D. It claims that humans evolved moral behaviors simply to ensure the survival of the fittest.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The moral argument states that "objective moral values and duties exist," and the reason humanity has a universal moral compass (knowing certain things are universally bad) is because that morality comes from a "transcendent moral law giver".
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-III-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-32b1015e-f0f6.md (00:16-01:10)

Q36. What is the fundamental conclusion of the ontological argument?
A. God exists only as a comforting psychological construct in the human imagination.
B. Because God is defined as the greatest possible being, and a being existing in reality is greater than one existing only in imagination, God must exist in reality.
C. God's existence can only be proven through physical, archaeological evidence.
D. God is a universal energy that permeates all living things, rather than a specific being.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The ontological argument defines God as the "greatest possible being imaginable." Because a being that exists in reality is greater than one only in imagination, the conclusion is that if you can conceive of this greatest being, "God must exist in reality".
REF: IS-THERE-A-GOD-III-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-32b1015e-f0f6.md (06:59-09:44)

Q37. What point does Paul make in 1 Corinthians 15:12-14 regarding the resurrection?
A. That the resurrection is a helpful but optional belief for mature Christians.
B. That if Christ is not risen, Christian preaching is vain and faith is in vain, leaving believers still in their sins.
C. That the resurrection only applies to the spirit, not the physical body.
D. That Jesus only appeared to resurrect to inspire the disciples' moral teachings.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: Quoting 1 Corinthians 15:12-14, the speaker notes Paul's argument: "if Christ be not risen, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is also in vain... you are still in your sins," showing the resurrection is the foundation of the faith.
REF: DID-JESUS-RISE-FROM-THE-DEAD-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-8fb9b97d-ffc1.md (03:05-03:50)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: 1 Corinthians 15:12–14 | Also cited in lesson segment: 1 Timothy 3

Q38. In the Old Testament Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), what did the "scapegoat" symbolize in relation to Christ?
A. It represented the Jewish leaders who rejected Jesus.
B. It represented the believers who would spread the gospel to the wilderness.
C. It represented the sacrifice for the high priest's personal sins before he could enter the Holy of Holies.
D. It prefigured Christ carrying the iniquities and rebellious acts of the people away into a solitary place.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The speaker explains that on the Day of Atonement, the high priest confessed the iniquities of Israel over the live goat (the scapegoat), which carried those sins away into the wilderness. This served as a type and shadow representing Jesus taking away the sins of the world.
REF: DID-JESUS-RISE-FROM-THE-DEAD-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-8fb9b97d-ffc1.md (11:18-12:06)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: Leviticus 16

Q39. According to Hebrews 9, how is Christ’s sacrifice different from the Old Testament high priest’s sacrifice?
A. Christ entered the holy place once and for all by His own blood, rather than entering yearly with the blood of animals.
B. Christ required the blood of a perfect bull to atone for His human weaknesses before entering heaven.
C. Christ did not offer blood, but instead offered moral teachings to secure redemption.
D. Christ must return to heaven repeatedly to renew His sacrifice for new sins.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: Referencing Hebrews 9, the speaker explains that unlike the Old Testament high priest who entered yearly with animal blood, Christ "entered the most holy place once and for all by his own blood, thus obtaining... eternal redemption".
REF: DID-JESUS-RISE-FROM-THE-DEAD-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-a8a24fd0-8a8b.md (00:51-01:48)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: Hebrews 9

Q40. How does the Islamic "substitution theory" explain the crucifixion of Jesus?
A. It claims Jesus willingly substituted Himself for Barabbas on the cross.
B. It claims Jesus was substituted with a sacrificial lamb at the last minute.
C. It claims Jesus was crucified, but substituted His divine spirit for a human one before dying.
D. It claims Jesus was not crucified at all; instead, someone else (often suggested as Judas) was made to resemble Him and was killed in His place.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The speaker cites Surah 4:159, explaining the Islamic substitution theory claims "they did not kill him nor did they crucify him, but another was made to resemble him," with some interpretations suggesting Judas was crucified in His place.
REF: DID-JESUS-RISE-FROM-THE-DEAD-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-a8a24fd0-8a8b.md (08:15-10:03)

Q41. What does the "Swoon Theory" claim about the resurrection of Jesus?
A. It claims Jesus was never nailed to the cross, but only tied to it.
B. It claims Jesus lost consciousness and fainted on the cross, but later revived in the tomb and survived.
C. It claims Jesus died, but the disciples hallucinated His resurrection because they swooned from grief.
D. It claims the Roman soldiers swooned and fell asleep, allowing thieves to steal the body.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The Swoon theory (from Ahmadiyya Islam) claims "Jesus was crucified, but he didn't actually die, that he merely swooned. He lost consciousness and he fainted... later he was revived in the tomb," arguing no resurrection miracle occurred.
REF: DID-JESUS-RISE-FROM-THE-DEAD-III-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-8a8d1adc-a011.md (04:08-05:06)
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: John 1:1

Q42. Why does the "Conspiracy or Fraud Theory" fail regarding the disciples' claims of the resurrection?
A. The disciples were too uneducated to invent a complex lie.
B. The Romans immediately found the stolen body, exposing the fraud.
C. People do not willingly die for a lie they invented themselves, and the early apostles faced execution without recanting.
D. The disciples were eventually paid by the Romans to confess they stole the body.
ANSWER: C

Q44. Why is it highly significant that the Gospels record women as the first eyewitnesses of the empty tomb?
A. It fulfilled a specific Old Testament prophecy about women discovering the Messiah.
B. It proved that the Roman guards were afraid of women.
C. In the first-century Jewish context, the testimony of women was considered invalid in court, meaning writers fabricating a story would never have used women as their primary witnesses.
D. The disciples were busy hiding in Galilee and sent the women to check the tomb.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The speaker explains that due to "widespread misogyny" in the ancient world, women's testimony was often considered invalid (as noted by Josephus and the Talmud). Therefore, "the last detail that a first century writer who is trying to fabricate a convincing story would have invented" is having women as the first witnesses, suggesting it was recorded simply because "it actually happened".

Q48. How does the lesson explain the apparent discrepancy between Matthew and Acts regarding the death of Judas Iscariot?

ANSWER: B

Q75. How does the lesson define the origin and composition of the Bible?

ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: Pastor Dolapo defines the Bible: "from the Latin word tabiblia, and it means a collection of books... written by over 40 authors. And within the space of 2000 years... their writings still form a unified salvation story".
REF: IS-THE-BIBLE-TRUE-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-2-mp4-4de941bf-ab47.md (01:14-01:37)

Q76. What was the significance of the Book of Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls?
A. It proved that Isaiah had originally predicted the rise of the Roman Empire.
B. It contained completely different theological teachings compared to modern Bibles.
C. It predated the previously oldest available manuscript by 1100 years yet maintained 95% accuracy, proving the reliable transmission of the text.
D. It was the only scroll in the cave written in perfect Greek.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The lesson notes that the Dead Sea Scroll of Isaiah (dating to 75 BC) was compared with the previously earliest manuscript (which was 1100 years later), and they discovered "it maintains 95% accuracy," with the 5% being mere spelling differences.
REF: IS-THE-BIBLE-TRUE-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-2-mp4-4de941bf-ab47.md (04:02-05:04)

Q77. What information does the Babylonian Talmud provide regarding Jesus that supports the Biblical account?
A. It confirms that He travelled to India during His teenage years.
B. It details the execution of a man named Yeshua, suggesting he was hung on the eve of the Passover.
C. It states that He successfully led a Jewish rebellion against the Romans.
D. It claims He was never crucified but lived to an old age in Egypt.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The speaker mentions that the Babylonian Talmud (Jewish rabbinic writing) helps us know about "the execution of a man called Yeshua... and suggests that he was hung on the eve of the Passover," which aligns with the New Testament.
REF: IS-THE-BIBLE-TRUE-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-2-mp4-8439008d-8508.md (01:10-02:15)

Q78. What Old Testament archaeological evidence is mentioned that validates the events recorded during King Hezekiah's reign?
A. The discovery of Goliath's armor in the valley of Elah.
B. The preservation of Noah's Ark on Mount Ararat.
C. The discovery of Hezekiah's tunnel, built during an Assyrian siege to protect Jerusalem's water supply.
D. The ruins of the Tower of Babel in modern-day Iraq.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The speaker points to Hezekiah's tunnel (2 Kings 20:20), explaining that during an Assyrian siege against Jerusalem, "King Hezekiah built a tunnel to protect the water supply in Jerusalem. That exact tunnel... still exists today".

Q79. How does Abraham’s intercession in Genesis 18 demonstrate that God's character is fundamentally good and just?
A. Abraham reminded God of a strict legal contract they had signed.
B. Abraham challenged God on His justice, knowing His reputation, by asking, "shall the judge of the world not do what is right?"
C. Abraham rebuked God for causing the flood.
D. Abraham proved that God had no right to judge the people of Sodom.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The lesson highlights that people in the Bible have challenged God based on His justice. Abraham, when negotiating for Sodom and Gomorrah, relied on God's integrity, asking, "shall the judge of the world not do what is right?".
REF: THEODICY-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-2-mp4-54713388-2eb8.md (04:19-04:24)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: Genesis 18 | Also cited in lesson segment: Exodus 33

Q80. What parallel does the lesson draw between Abraham’s negotiation and Moses's actions in Exodus 32/33?
A. Both men requested that God completely destroy the nations around Israel.
B. Both men used their knowledge of God's goodness to intercede for rebellious people when God expressed anger.
C. Both men were punished by God for asking too many questions.
D. Both men wrote lengthy philosophical treatises on theodicy.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: Similar to Abraham, when the Israelites were "stiff necked" and built the golden calf, Moses interceded on their behalf. The speaker notes Moses told God, "I know you. You're a good guy... You are not wicked," appealing to God's inherent goodness.
REF: THEODICY-I-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-2-mp4-54713388-2eb8.md (04:35-05:14)
BIBLE: Also cited in lesson segment: Exodus 33 | Added from online research: Exodus 32:1–14 (https://www.esv.org/verses/Exodus+32:1%E2%80%9314/)

Q81. How does the lesson contextualize Romans 8:28 ("all things work together for good") in light of suffering?
A. It means that every bad thing that happens is actually good and shouldn't cause pain.
B. It means that God promises believers will eventually become wealthy in this lifetime to make up for their pain.
C. It clarifies that while not all things are inherently good, an all-knowing, sovereign God can work all outcomes toward His ultimate good for those who love Him.
D. It suggests that suffering is an illusion that believers must ignore through positive confession.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The speaker emphasizes that "the verse did not say all things are good" or that "all suffering is immediately understandable." Rather, because God is sovereign, all-knowing, and all-good, "he can work all those outcomes for his ultimate good".
REF: THEODICY-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-345e7215-afe4.md (11:24)
BIBLE: Confirmed in lesson and deck: Romans 8:28

Q82. How does the speaker use the analogy of a "building site" to explain God's plan amidst perceived chaos?
A. A building site is always clean and orderly, just as God's plans are always clearly understood by humans.
B. A building site is chaotic with noise, dust, and incongruous materials, showing that current disorder is not the absence of design, but the presence of an unfinished design.
C. A building site frequently collapses, representing how human free will destroys God's plans.
D. A building site proves that humans must labor in sweat and pain to achieve salvation.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The speaker compares suffering to a building site filled with "noise," "dust," and materials that "look absolutely nothing like the final structure." The key point is that "disorder is not necessarily the absence of design. Many times it's the presence of a design you cannot yet see".
REF: THEODICY-II-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-345e7215-afe4.md (08:05-08:26)

Q83. What highly troubling details about Sodom and Gomorrah does the lesson cite to justify God’s judgment of the cities?
A. They had abandoned agriculture to focus on making weapons of war.
B. They worshipped fallen angels and built towering idols to them.
C. The entire male population possessed such a severe reprobate and violent sexual nature that they sought to assault visiting strangers, right from the city gates.
D. They charged exorbitant taxes to travelers crossing their borders.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The speaker describes the depth of Sodom's depravity, noting that "all the men in the city" had the proclivity to assault strangers. "They saw angels at the gates and wanted to rape them," illustrating the extreme wickedness that prompted God's judgment.
REF: THEODICY-III-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-8b09d75d-6ba0.md (07:13-07:56)

Q84. What historical event illustrates the danger of Israel failing to fully obey God's commands to drive out corrupt nations (like the Amalekites)?
A. The destruction of the second temple by the Romans in 70 AD.
B. The rise of Haman the Agagite during the Babylonian exile, who attempted to annihilate the entire Jewish race.
C. The enslavement of Israel in Egypt under Pharaoh.
D. The splitting of the kingdom into Israel and Judah.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The speaker uses Saul's failure to completely destroy the Amalekites (sparing Agag) as an example. Later, during the exile, "Haman the Agagite" wanted to "come and finish the work" and destroy the Jews, which would have prevented Jesus from coming to save humanity.
REF: THEODICY-III-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-8b09d75d-6ba0.md (10:17-10:57)

Q85. According to the lesson, why does human labor often involve intense struggle and frustration today?
A. Because humans forgot the original farming techniques used by Adam.
B. Because God desired for humans to build physical endurance.
C. It is a direct result of the curse in Genesis where God said, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread," following Adam's fall.
D. It is due entirely to modern economic systems and capitalism.
ANSWER: C
EXPLANATION: The speaker connects the struggle of human labor to the fall in Genesis, explaining that when God said, "cursed is the ground for thy sake... In the sweat of thy face, thou shalt eat bread," it meant that human labor now involves struggle as part of natural evil.
REF: THEODICY-IV-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-3877d1c1-564b.md (03:56-04:42)

Q86. How does the lesson frame the "now and not yet" reality of Christ's victory over evil and death?
A. Christ has won the final victory over death, but believers still live in a world with "pockets of resistance" (like sickness) while awaiting the complete physical manifestation of that victory.
B. Christ's victory will only begin once all believers become completely sinless.
C. Christ has not actually defeated evil yet; He is waiting for the Church to defeat it through political action.
D. Believers currently experience zero sickness or pain if their faith is genuine.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The speaker compares the current reality to winning a war where "there are still pockets of resistance... rebels still kicking up." Death is defeated, but on earth right now, "you might have to wake up every day and carry your cross," awaiting the final day when God wipes away every tear.
REF: THEODICY-IV-Celebration-Church-International-LMS-mp4-3877d1c1-564b.md (14:42-16:17)

Q87. Which point does the speaker use to challenge the hallucination theory of the resurrection appearances?
A. The theory says that one person saw Jesus once, at the tomb.
B. The theory requires the disciples to have stolen Jesus' body.
C. The reports describe a single appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem.
D. The speaker points to appearances over 40 days, including one to 500 people at once.
ANSWER: D
EXPLANATION: The speaker argues that a hallucination does not account for the reported appearances over 40 days, to different groups and locations, including the appearance to 500 people at one time.

Q88. How did the apostles initially respond to the women's report that Jesus had risen?
A. They immediately believed it and went to Galilee.
B. They assumed the authorities had moved Jesus' body.

D. They accused the women of stealing the body.
ANSWER: C

Q89. Which detail from the lesson supports the claim that Jesus' resurrection appearances were physical?
A. The disciples heard a voice but did not see Jesus.
B. Jesus showed his wounds and ate with the disciples.
C. The women returned with another report from the tomb.
D. The authorities announced that Jesus was alive.
ANSWER: B
EXPLANATION: The speaker points to Jesus showing Thomas his wounds and to Jesus eating with the disciples as evidence that they encountered him physically.

Q90. What did Jesus rebuke the Emmaus disciples for?
A. Being slow to believe what the prophets had said about the Messiah.
B. Expecting the Messiah to raise an army and expel Rome.
C. Returning to Jerusalem before the other disciples arrived.
D. Claiming that the tomb had never been empty.
ANSWER: A
EXPLANATION: The speaker recalls Jesus calling them foolish and slow to believe the prophets, who had taught that the Messiah must suffer and then enter his glory.
